title: The Tortoise That Wears Its Bones on the Outside

blocks.prompt: The Shell Is Not a House
blocks.text: A turtle swims. A tortoise walks. That is the big difference between them. A tortoise lives on land, in dry grass and warm sun. Here is the part most people get wrong. The shell is not a house. The tortoise cannot climb out and leave it behind. The shell is joined right onto its ribs and its backbone. It is part of the tortoise, the way your bones are part of you. When something scary comes close, the tortoise pulls its head and legs inside and waits. A tortoise has no teeth at all. It has a hard beak, and it snips grass and flowers with it. It is in no hurry. Some tortoises live for more than a hundred years.

blocks.prompt: Wearing Your Bones on the Outside
blocks.text: Almost everyone gets the shell wrong. A tortoise does not live in its shell the way you live in a house. It cannot crawl out and leave the shell behind. The shell is the tortoise. Under the surface, about fifty bones are fused together into one curved case, and those bones are the tortoise's own ribs and backbone, flattened out and spread wide. On top of the bone sit hard plates called scutes. Scutes are made of keratin, which is the same stuff as your fingernails. Here is the clever bit. The scutes do not line up with the joins in the bone underneath. They cross over them, the way bricks cross over each other in a wall, and that crossing makes the whole shell much harder to break. The shell is also alive. Blood moves through it. Nerves run through it. A tortoise can feel a soft scratch on its back, and it can feel a crack. So the shell is not armor that a tortoise puts on in the morning. It is a tortoise, wearing its bones on the outside.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Its ribs are locked into the shell and cannot move
It breathes using belly muscles instead
Ectotherm: it borrows its heat from the sun
A desert tortoise stores water in its bladder
It can go over a year without a drink
It walks about a fifth of a mile per hour

blocks.prompt: Breathing Inside a Box
blocks.text: Sealing your ribs into a solid box solves one problem and creates another. The shell keeps a tortoise safe from teeth and claws. It also makes breathing impossible in the ordinary way. You breathe by swinging your ribs outward, which makes room and pulls air into your lungs. A tortoise cannot swing its ribs. They are locked into the shell and they do not move at all. So the tortoise breathes with its belly. Its lungs are fixed to the inside of the roof of the shell, and sheets of muscle underneath push the tortoise's insides up against them to squeeze the air out, then pull away to let air rush back in. Every breath a tortoise takes, it takes by shoving its own organs around. Everything else about a tortoise runs slow too. It is ectothermic, which means it does not burn food to make its own heat. It borrows heat from the sun instead. A cold tortoise is a stiff, sleepy tortoise, so mornings are for basking: lying flat and wide, soaking up warmth before the day's work of eating grass. Running slow is expensive in speed and cheap in fuel, and that trade pays off in odd places. A desert tortoise in the Mojave spends most of its life underground in a burrow, out of the killing heat, doing almost nothing. It stores water in its bladder and drinks it back out of itself over the following months. It can go more than a year without finding a puddle. It travels at about a fifth of a mile per hour. It may also still be alive when the child who first spotted it has grandchildren of her own.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Giant tortoises walk about a fifth of a mile per hour
A resting heart beats only a few times a minute
Whaling ships stored them alive for a year
Domed shells graze low, saddleback shells reach high
Their ancestors floated to the Galapagos
One Aldabra tortoise drifted to Africa in 2004

blocks.prompt: Slow Is a Strategy
blocks.text: Speed costs fuel. A cheetah's sprint is paid for in meat, and meat has to be chased and caught and sometimes lost. The tortoise opted out of that entire economy. It eats grass, weeds, cactus, and fallen fruit, none of which run away, and it turns that low-grade fuel into a life measured in human generations rather than years. The trade shows up everywhere in its body. A giant tortoise walks at roughly a fifth of a mile per hour. Its resting heart beats only a few times a minute. It can go months without eating and barely notice. That last ability is harmless in the wild. It turned out to be a catastrophe. In the 1700s and 1800s, whaling and sealing ships worked out that they could stack living tortoises upside down in a dark hold, feed them nothing, water them nothing, and still be carving fresh meat a year later. Ships took them by the hundreds. Somewhere between one and two hundred thousand tortoises were carried off the Galapagos Islands. Charles Darwin's own ship loaded about thirty of them and ate them on the voyage home, throwing the empty shells over the side. Darwin missed something on those islands, and he knew it afterward. The vice-governor, an Englishman named Nicholas Lawson, told him he could look at any tortoise and name the island it came from. Darwin did not take the remark seriously enough at the time to keep the shells, and he never quite forgave himself. Lawson was right. On the wet, high islands, where grass grows at ankle height, tortoises have smooth domed shells and short necks, and they simply graze. On the dry, low islands, where the only green thing is a cactus pad held up out of reach, the front of the shell rises into a shape like a saddle, the neck is long, and the animal reaches up. Same ancestor, different island, different body. The ancestor arrived by floating. Tortoises sink in fresh water, but a giant one rides high in salt water with its head up, and it does not need to eat while it drifts. One Aldabra tortoise washed ashore on the coast of Tanzania in 2004, crusted with barnacles, alive, after drifting several hundred miles. That is how a South American tortoise reached islands six hundred miles offshore, roughly three million years ago, and slowly became something new. Slow is not the same as safe. Slow means the bill arrives later, and somebody else usually delivers it.

6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Tortoise That Wears Its Bones on the Outside

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The only animal with its shoulders inside its own ribs
Eunotosaurus, 260 million years old, had broad flat ribs
Odontochelys had a belly shell, teeth, and no top shell
Negligible senescence: the risk of dying barely climbs with age
Jonathan the tortoise hatched around 1832
Counting scute rings does not give you a tortoise's age

blocks.prompt: The Skeleton Turned Inside Out
blocks.text: Every animal with a backbone is built to roughly the same plan, and the plan has rules. One of the oldest is this: the shoulder blades sit outside the ribcage. Yours do. A dog's do. A bird's do. A tortoise's do not. Its shoulders are inside its own ribs, an arrangement so strange that for most of two centuries nobody could explain how it came about. Embryos gave the answer. Watch a tortoise develop inside its egg and you see the ribs, instead of curving downward to build a basket, grow outward and flatten into a disc, and the shoulder is simply left on the inside as the disc spreads over it. The shell is not armor bolted onto a reptile. It is a reptile's own skeleton turned inside out. The fossils agree, and they tell the story backwards from what you would guess. Eunotosaurus, about 260 million years old, has no shell at all, just ribs that are suspiciously broad and flat, apparently for bracing the body of an animal that dug. Odontochelys, about forty million years younger, has a complete bottom shell, a full set of teeth, and no top shell whatsoever. The belly was armored first. That ordering suggests the whole structure began as protection from below, from something attacking upward out of the water, and only later closed over the back. Closing over the back created a problem. Locked ribs cannot pump. Every other reptile breathes by flexing its ribcage, and a tortoise's ribcage does not flex, so it evolved a workaround: sheets of muscle that haul its own organs away from its lungs to inhale and shove them back to exhale. It breathes by rearranging its insides. This is not elegant, but it has run without interruption for over two hundred million years, which is longer than snakes have existed, longer than birds, longer than flowers. What the shell bought was time. An animal that cannot easily be bitten in half has no need to breed fast and die young, and tortoise biology followed accordingly. They mature late, reproduce for decades, and age so slowly that biologists genuinely argue about whether they meaningfully age at all. The technical term is negligible senescence: the chance of dying does not measurably climb with each passing year the way it does for you and me. A hundred-year-old tortoise is not the equivalent of a hundred-year-old man. It is closer to an adult in no particular hurry. The record holder is a Seychelles giant tortoise named Jonathan, who hatched around 1832 and has spent most of his life on a lawn on the island of Saint Helena, in the South Atlantic. He was already fully grown when he arrived in 1882. He has outlasted the invention of the telephone, the airplane, and the computer, along with the entire lives of every person who ever loaded a tortoise onto a ship. In 2022 the island threw him a party for his 190th birthday, which made him the oldest land animal anybody has ever kept a record of. He had gone blind by then, and lost his sense of smell, and was being hand-fed cabbage and cucumber on the lawn, and by every account he was doing fine. Guessing a tortoise's age is famously unreliable, incidentally. People count the rings on the scutes the way you would count tree rings, and it does not work. The rings track how well the animal was eating, not how many times the Earth went around the sun. A tortoise with a good year lays down a wide ring. A tortoise with a bad one lays down almost nothing. This design has survived every mass extinction since the Triassic. What it never had to survive was us. Sailors emptied whole islands. Habitat loss came next. A body built to shrug off a hundred years of bad luck cannot shrug off a bulldozer, and the shell that answered every problem the world threw at it for two hundred million years had no answer at all for a species that could simply pick it up and carry it away.
